## *Homo sapiens* have been around for 300,000 years
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:210px; LEFT:5px; WIDTH:525px; HEIGHT:325px" SRC="images/homosapien.png">

<div style="float: right; width: 50%;">

* **Survived mostly as foragers or hunter-gatherers**
    + thorough knowledge of local botany
    
<br/>

* **~10,000 years ago: foraging to farming**
    
<br/>

* **Agriculture arose in several places**
    + the notion that the fertile cresent was the start of agriculture is now quite true

<br/>

* **Farming = basis of advanced civilizations**
    + old and new worlds
 
 </div>
 
## Foraging societies
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 52%;">

* **Foragers gather food provided by nature**
    + still practiced by indigenous cultures
    + https://youtu.be/Pro6X_Kc5wA
    
<br/>

* **In Homo spp; smarter, cooperative foraging for high-calorie, high-quality foods fed more energy to the body, which made it possible to afford and then favor bigger, more expensive brains!!**

<br/>

* **Does NOT imply a vegetarian diet**
    + Arctic Inuits = only meat
    + Hadza of Tanzania = vegetarian
    + !Kung of S. Africa = plants, eggs, fish, meat

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:575px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:350px" SRC="images/gather.jpg">

## Early foragers
<hr>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:625px; WIDTH:375px; HEIGHT:475px" SRC="images/plants.jpg">

<div style="float: left; width: 55%;">

* **Fossil evidence reveals the diets of early foragers**
    + charred seeds & preserved fruits
    + bones, shells & feathers

<br/>
    
* **Coprolites: fossilized poop!**
    + pollen forensics helps recreate diets

<br/>

* **Tool remains and cave drawings reveal meat diet**

<br/>

* **17,000 years ago: Wadi-Kubbaaniya in Nile Valley**
    + 25 plant species
    + tubers of grasses with high starch
    + plants needed to be 'processed'

</div>

## Modern foragers
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 55%;">

* **Evidence from key modern foraging societies**
    + !Kung from tropical African savannas
    + most studied remaining gatherer communities

<br/>

* **10,000 years of foraging history**
    + continuing today
    
* **!Kung forage over 100 species of plants and 50 animal species**
    + 2355 kilocalories a day
    + 96 grams of protein
    + adequate vitamins and minerals
 
 <br/>
 
* **Dedicated division of labor along gender lines**
    + foraging = 2.5 days a week

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:5px; WIDTH:475px; HEIGHT:375px" SRC="images/kung.jpg">

## Paleo diet (Caveman's diet)
<hr>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

* **Recent diet trends relate to foraging past**
    + similar to hunter-gatherer periods

<br/>
    
* **No dairy, refined grains or sugars or legumes**
    + none available for past foragers
    
<br/>

* **Eat large quantities of meats, fruits, nuts, root vegetables and honey**
    + human body 'adapted' for this diet

<br/>   

* **Based on the fallacy that humans bodies have not evolved**
    + lactase gene now 'stays on' passed infancy
    + assumes one kind of forager diet

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:600px; WIDTH:450px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/paleo.jpg">

## Agriculture: Revolution of evolution?
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>


<div style="float: right; width: 63%;">

* **Archaeology shows plant cultivation started ~10,000 years ago**
 
<br/>
 
* **Agriculture flourished in Near East, Far East and Mesoamererica for thousands of years**

<br/>

* **Question: Why the switch?**
    + a brilliant sage saw the power of seeds?
    + was the transition a revolution?
    + did a gradual cultural evolution take place?
    + was it climate related?
    
</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:25px; WIDTH:350px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/revolution.jpg">

## End of an ice age....Neolithic Revolution
<hr>
<br/>

**Around 10,000 to 12,000 years ago, the Earth's climate began to warm significantly, marking the end of the last glacial period**

<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 52%;">

**Created a more stable environment with a longer growing season and more varied plant life**

<br/>

**Climate shifts led to wildfires and soil erosion, which may have created fertile valley basins**

<br/>

**Allowed humans to stay in one area and develop farming/animal husbandry instead of relying on foraging**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:275px; LEFT:40px; WIDTH:440px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/dryas.png">

## Early sites of agriculture
<hr>
<br/>

* **Farming didn’t appear in one place and spread everywhere**

<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

* **Started independently multiple times:**
    + Fertile Crescent (wheat/barley) 
    + China (millet/rice)
    + New Guinea (taro/bananas)
    + Africa (sorghum/millet/rice)
    + Mesoamerica (maize/beans/squash)
    + Andes (potato/quinoa/llama)
    + Eastern N. America (native seed crops)

<br/>

* **Those cores radiated outward and mixed**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:230px; LEFT:510px; WIDTH:600px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/map.png">

## The Near East: Fertile Crescent (~11,500 years ago)
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 48%;">

* **Iran, Iran, Turkey, Syria, Lebanon and Israel**
    + some of the oldest sites of agriculture

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:550px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/fertile.png">

## The Near East: Fertile Crescent (~11,500 years ago)
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 48%;">

* **Iran, Iran, Turkey, Syria, Lebanon and Israel**
    + some of the oldest sites of agriculture
    
<br/>

* **Animals domesticated first**
    + sheep, cattle, goats, and cats!

<br/>

* **Plants: Cereals einkorn and emmer wheat, barley, legumes like lentil, pea, and chickpea**

<br/>

* **Jarmo site: 24 houses with ~150 people**
    + 9,000 years ago
    + domesticated grains + foraging

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:575px; WIDTH:450px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/fertile2.png">

## The Far East: Yellow and Yangtze River Valleys
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

* **Rice cultivation began 11,500 years ago**
    + farming then spread up- and down streams

<br/>

* **Domestication of millet, hemp, pigs, cattle & poultry after rice**

<br/>

* **Silkworm domestication 5,000 years ago**
    + 354 genes differ between domestic & wild

<br/>

* **Horse domestication 5,000 years ago**
    + Batai from plains of Central Asia
    
</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:250px; LEFT:575px; WIDTH:475px; HEIGHT:350px" SRC="images/yellow.jpg">

## The New World: Mexico and Peru
<hr>

<div style="float: left; width: 99%;">

* **Timing of plant domestication matches Fertile Crescent and Far East**

<br/>

* **Domestication of plants dominant**
    + squash, corn, peppers, beans, avocado & potatoes

<br/>

</div>

<div style="float: left; width: 48%;">

* **Fewer animals domesticated**
    + dogs, turkeys, alpacas & guinea pigs
    
<br/>

* **Archaeology points to Peru for farming origins**

<br/>

* **Corn domestication in central Mexico**
    + 5,000 years ago (found in caves)
    + arrived in US ~2,000 years ago

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:295px; LEFT:580px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:385px" SRC="images/corn.jpg">

## The role of Appalachia in the history of agriculture
<hr>

* **Indigenous peoples in and around the Appalachian region were farming and domesticating their own plants**
    + called the Eastern Agricultural Complex.

<br/>

* **Key native plants were managed, tended, and selectively bred in river valleys that cut through the Appalachian region**
    + Ohio River, Tennessee River, Cumberland River
    + goosefoot seeds, sumpweed seeds (oil), 
    + sunflower (seeds and oil), squash, barley (starch)
    
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 51%;">

* **Patchy geography supported lots of parallel small-scale domestication experiments**

<br/>

* **Maize, beans, and squash (“Three Sisters”) became staples later**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:330px; LEFT:620px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:350px" SRC="images/eac.png">

## Theory of Latitudinal Spread (Jared Diamond)
<hr>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:225px; LEFT:570px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:300px" SRC="images/latspread.jpg">

<div style="float: left; width: 55%;">

* **Theory of development & spread of agriculture**
    + certain areas of the world & not it others
    + 0.7 miles per year
    
<br/>
 
* **East-West orientation in Eurasia**
    + crops & livestock outward from fertile crescent
    
<br/>

* **North-South orientation in Americas**
    + crops from Mexico to US (.5 miles/year)
    + llama spread Peru to Ecuador (.2 miles/year)

<br/>

</div>

<div style="float: left; width: 99%;">

* **Direction of domestication interacts with climate!**
    + moving the agricultural knowledge N-S includes big climate shifts, which slowed spread
    
</div>

## European Stone Age
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 59%;">

* **Farming spread from Near East**
    + first to Turkey, Greece and Bulgaria
    + ~7500 years ago farming spread to rest of Europe
    
<br/>
 
* **DNA from ancient European foragers compared to earliest farmers**
    + 15,000 - 4,300 years ago
    + *not related*!!!
    
<br/>

* **DNA also compared to modern Europeans**
    + modern Europeans related to farmers, not foragers
    + first farmers were immigrants, that spread agriculture
    
</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:635px; WIDTH:425px; HEIGHT:375px" SRC="images/europe.jpeg">

## Global population tied to agriculture
<hr>
**The human population increased from  ~5 million to 50 million during and shortly after the first agricultural revolution. This increase was due to a more stable and abundant food supply from farming, which allowed for a larger, settled population that could also support higher birth rates. **

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:150px; WIDTH:800px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/humanpop.jpg">

## Characteristics of domesticated plants
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

* **Domesticated plants genetically distinct**
    + artificial vs natural selection

<br/>

* **Wild plants: selection pressures from the environment**
    + traits have 'survival value'

<br/>

* **Domesticated plants: traits are breed to suit human needs**
    + not always advantageous
    
<br/>

* **Example: Ensheathing husks in corn or non-shattering heads wheat**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:560px; WIDTH:450px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/sheath.png">

## Origins of key domesticated plants
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:190px; LEFT:5px; WIDTH:600px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/croporigins.png">

<div style="float: right; width: 41%;">

* **Vavilov (Russian botanist) proposed 8 centers of crop domestication**
    + highest diversity = origin
    + wild strains key for genetic diversity
    
<br/>

* **Trading & migration expanded range of crops**

<br/>

* **Some crops do better in new areas**
    + most of US crops are not native
    + coffee native to Ethiopia

</div>
